title.title: Industries & Case Studies
title.subtitle: Where smart contracts run in real industries, including the cases that failed

discussion.title: Discussion: which industry hurts most?
discussion.lead: Before the five deep-dives: where does today's process cause the most pain — and would code enforcing the rules actually fix it?
questions: Of the five verticals on the next slide — finance, gaming & NFTs, real-world assets, supply chain, certification — which slow or expensive process have you personally run into? Who gets paid for that friction today?
Which single party in that process does everyone currently have to trust? What happens when they fail, cheat or shut down?
If the rules were code instead of a contract between people, what would still need a human to decide?
discussion.note: The Section 4 framework and the Section 7 assignment start from this question.

examples.name: Uniswap
examples.desc: Any wallet swaps thousands of tokens in one on-chain call; the contract quotes the price and never takes custody of user funds.

examples.name: CoW Swap
examples.desc: Users sign an intent; solvers batch and match orders off-chain and settle them in one transaction, with MEV protection built in.

examples.name: USDC on an L2
examples.desc: A SWIFT wire takes 3–5 days and $25–50 plus FX spread; a stablecoin on Base or Arbitrum settles wallet-to-wallet in seconds — irreversibly, and the on/off-ramp still needs a bank.

nftReal.heading: NFTs in production
nftReal.subtitle: A major studio running a game economy on NFTs, and a lender that takes NFTs as collateral.

columns.title: Champions Tactics: Grimoria Chronicles
columns.tag: Strategic Innovation Lab · launched Oct 2024 on the Oasys chain
points: 75,000 Champion NFTs sold in a capped drop, funding operations upfront
Players battle squads in PvP; victories earn on-chain reward tokens redeemable for gear
Every secondary sale routes a 5% royalty to Ubisoft and collaborating artists — when the marketplace honours it
The servers, artwork and matchmaking are still Ubisoft's — the NFT only covers who owns the item
columns.footnote: The chain records who owns the item; the game is still Ubisoft's.

columns.title: Borrow against an NFT without selling it
points: The NFT is locked in a contract; if the loan defaults, the contract hands it to the lender — no court, no collections agency
Zharta grew to 300+ loans at ~13.6% APR with terms up to two years, secured by on-chain collateral
Rentals follow the same pattern: lend the asset to a new player and split the earnings automatically
The weak point is pricing — an illiquid NFT can lose most of its value before any liquidation fires
columns.footnote: If a digital asset has value, lending, renting and yield can be built around it — with the same liquidation risks as any collateral.

rwaReal.heading: Tokenised assets in production
rwaReal.subtitle: Where real-world assets already live on-chain — and what still happens off-chain.

columns.title: BlackRock BUIDL · Securitize · BNY Mellon
points: Tokenised money-market and credit funds issued on Ethereum, Polygon and Avalanche
Each token is a share in an off-chain fund; KYC/AML runs through on-chain compliance modules
24/7 settlement instead of T+1 / T+2, and fractional access to institutional products
columns.footnote: The token settles in seconds; the fund share it represents is still governed by a prospectus and a transfer agent.

columns.title: Sweden · Brickblock · Zurich Bahnhofstrasse
columns.tag: Land registry pilot and real-estate tokens
points: Sweden's land-registry pilot cut title registration from about 4 months to a few days (€100M+ estimated yearly savings)
Brickblock (Frankfurt) issued property tokens on Ethereum under BaFin supervision
A Zurich Bahnhofstrasse building was tokenised through a Swiss GmbH — investors receive rent and trade shares under FINMA guidelines
columns.footnote: EU MiCA (2024) gives crypto-assets one legal framework across 27 states — the clarity these pilots were waiting for.

columns.title: Automated mortgages & tokenised collateral
points: The contract holds funds, tracks repayments, applies late penalties and liquidates collateral by itself
Borrowing against tokenised securities keeps market exposure while unlocking liquidity; margin calls settle instantly
Limitation: the house itself still changes hands through a legal title transfer off-chain
columns.footnote: The further right on the spectrum, the more the token depends on a legal wrapper — and the wrapper is where the risk sits.

scReal.heading: Provenance and shipping documents in production
scReal.subtitle: Three consortia where rivals agreed to write to one shared record — luxury, food and global shipping.

columns.title: LVMH · Aura Blockchain Consortium
columns.tag: Louis Vuitton, Prada, Cartier and partners
points: Every handbag, watch or perfume gets a digital passport on a permissioned chain: materials, production date, ownership changes
Shoppers scan the NFC or QR tag to see provenance; resale platforms and after-sales read the same brand-verified record
Goal: make counterfeits detectable and keep the resale market honest
columns.footnote: Competitors share infrastructure because none of them could fight counterfeiting alone.

columns.title: Carrefour BIO · organic chicken
columns.tag: Consumer-facing QR code on every pack
points: Farmers, processors and logistics partners upload at each hand-off: breed, farm, feed, antibiotic-free status, slaughter date, transport temperature
The record is locked on a permissioned ledger; a shopper's scan shows the full trail
Payoff: faster recalls and a stronger organic label
columns.footnote: The chain proves who entered what and when — it cannot prove the chicken was actually organic.

columns.title: GSBN electronic Bills of Lading
columns.tag: COSCO · Hapag-Lloyd · OOCL · Hutchison Ports · PSA
points: Bills of Lading used to travel as couriered paper — lost, forged or delayed for weeks
Each eBL is cryptographically signed, shared in seconds and tamper-evident; contracts notify customs on loading and release goods on ownership transfer
Live since 2021: 2M+ containers processed, document turnaround cut from days to hours
columns.footnote: Same industry as TradeLens — this one works because the carriers own it together.

certReal.heading: Verifiable records in production
certReal.subtitle: A government, a university and a luxury consortium — all using the chain so anyone can verify a record without phoning the issuer.

columns.title: KSI blockchain (Guardtime)
points: Permissioned hash-chain guaranteeing the integrity of the land registry, business registry, court system and health records
"Keyless" signatures: any later change to a historical record is detectable — even by a future government insider
Blockchain treated as infrastructure, not a product; the same backbone supports e-Residency and X-Road
columns.footnote: "History cannot be rewritten by anybody and the authenticity of electronic data can be guaranteed."

columns.title: Blockcerts digital diplomas
points: Verifying a diploma used to mean emailing the registrar and waiting days; fake credentials are a multi-billion-dollar market
MIT issued blockchain-anchored certificates to 100+ graduates; employers scan a QR code and verify instantly
Graduates hold their own credential — the university no longer sits in every verification
columns.footnote: An open standard since adopted by universities worldwide.

columns.title: Product authenticity certificates
points: Each item carries a unique on-chain certificate: origin, materials, manufacturing date, ownership history
Buyers verify instantly, resellers prove provenance, after-sales is tied to verified ownership
Counterfeiters cannot forge the history — but they can still copy the bag
columns.footnote: Collaborative rather than competitive infrastructure — the same consortium we met in supply chain.

caseGallery.heading: Cross-industry case gallery
caseGallery.subtitle: Five production deployments in one view — the problem, what runs on-chain, the headline result. Section 4 adds three more lessons.

items.name: Home Depot
items.problem: Supplier disputes over damaged or late goods took 3–5 weeks of emails and paper reconciliation.
items.solution: Purchase orders, deliveries and invoices on one shared ledger; contracts auto-match deliveries to POs and flag discrepancies instantly.

items.name: Propy
items.problem: Closing a property sale takes 30–60 days and about 6% in intermediary fees.
items.solution: The deed sits in an LLC; an ERC-721 NFT represents the LLC, and escrow releases funds only once title is confirmed.

items.name: California DMV
items.problem: 42M paper vehicle titles — easy to lose or forge, and a 2–3 hour DMV visit to transfer one.
items.solution: Each title becomes an NFT on a permissioned Avalanche subnet; transfers and lien releases are blockchain transactions.

items.name: Walmart
items.problem: Tracing contaminated lettuce to its farm took 7 days; whole categories were pulled from shelves.
items.solution: Farmers, packers, distributors and stores record each hand-off on IBM Food Trust; QR codes link the product to its provenance.

items.name: Santander
items.problem: Bond settlement across jurisdictions takes T+2 through a chain of intermediaries.
items.solution: A $20M bond issued on public Ethereum in 2019 with the cash leg tokenised too — end-to-end on-chain settlement.

poe.title: Proof of Existence
poe.subtitle: Hash a credential, anchor it on-chain, then verify it. The blockchain never sees the document — only the hash.
poe.verifyPlaceholderPrompt: Anchor a hash first, then come back here to verify a (possibly tampered) credential.
poe.verifyTextareaPlaceholder: Paste the document you want to verify…
poe.whyWorksBody: SHA-256 is deterministic: the same input always gives the same hash, and any change gives a completely different one. Anchoring the hash proves the document existed at that moment without revealing it.

pegSim.title: Stablecoin Peg Simulator
pegSim.subtitle: Pick a stablecoin design and apply market stress.
pegSim.shockLabel: Market shock — % of supply sold off
pegSim.shockDesc: Sudden sell pressure (a "bank run" event). 100% = entire supply hits the bid simultaneously.
pegSim.noteBody: these formulas are illustrative, not market models. Real peg dynamics involve liquidation cascades, market depth, redemption windows, and reflexive trading. The point:
pegSim.noteEmphasis: each design has a different failure mode

fiat.name: Fiat-backed
fiat.controlDesc: How much of circulating supply is provably backed in a bank/T-bills

crypto.name: Crypto-collateralized
crypto.controlDesc: Value of locked ETH (or other crypto) per $1 minted. 150% = $150 ETH backs $100 DAI

algo.name: Algorithmic
algo.controlDesc: Market-cap of the volatile sister token (LUNA-style) relative to the stablecoin supply

lessons.fiat: Fiat-backed stablecoins are only as trustworthy as their auditor. If reserves dip below 100%, a coordinated sell-off can break the peg — see USDC briefly de-pegging in March 2023 when SVB held $3.3B of its reserves.
lessons.crypto: Crypto-collateralized stablecoins survive shocks via liquidations — but only if the collateral ratio is comfortably above 100%. Drop below that during a flash crash and the protocol can't liquidate fast enough.
lessons.algo: Algorithmic stablecoins are vulnerable to reflexive death spirals: as the stable de-pegs, traders dump the sister token, which collapses, which removes the cushion. UST/LUNA wiped out $40B in May 2022.

exercise.title: Design Your Own Smart Contract
exercise.subtitle: Pick an industry, then think through each prompt before revealing the example answer.

prompts.0: What problem exists in {{industry}} that requires trust in an intermediary?
prompts.1: Who are the 2–3 parties involved? Who holds the funds or assets?
prompts.2: What event or condition triggers the smart contract to execute?
prompts.3: What does the contract do automatically when triggered?
prompts.4: What could go wrong? What is the single weakest point in this design?

Finance.pain: Cross-border payments take 3–5 days and cost 5–8% in fees
Finance.trigger: Sender deposits funds + recipient KYC confirmed
Finance.output: Funds released instantly to recipient in local currency
Finance.risk: Oracle needed for FX rate — potential manipulation

Supply Chain.pain: Invoice disputes between suppliers and retailers take 3–5 weeks to resolve
Supply Chain.trigger: Delivery scan confirmed + invoice matched to PO
Supply Chain.risk: IoT sensor data must come from a trusted oracle

Healthcare.pain: Patient consent for data sharing is paper-based and slow
Healthcare.output: Access token minted — Hospital B can read specific records
Healthcare.risk: Medical data itself must stay off-chain (privacy law)

Real Estate.pain: Property title transfer takes 30–60 days and costs 6% in intermediary fees
Real Estate.trigger: Full payment received + title search clear
Real Estate.output: Deed NFT transferred to buyer; funds released to seller
Real Estate.risk: Legal recognition of NFT as deed requires legislation

Government.pain: Benefit disbursements are slow and subject to fraud
Government.trigger: Eligibility criteria confirmed via verified credentials
Government.output: Benefit amount sent directly to citizen wallet
Government.risk: Off-chain identity verification is the weak point

Entertainment.pain: Music royalties take 18 months to reach artists through label chains
Entertainment.risk: High transaction volume — requires L2 or rollup

Insurance.pain: Flight delay claims require manual submission and 2–4 week payout
Insurance.output: Fixed payout sent automatically to traveller wallet
Insurance.risk: Oracle data quality is the single point of failure

Gaming.pain: In-game assets can be deleted or altered by the developer at any time
Gaming.trigger: Player purchases or earns item in-game
Gaming.output: NFT minted to player wallet — tradeable and permanent
Gaming.risk: Game server still centralised; contract only covers ownership

industriesIntro.heading: Smart Contracts Across Industries
industriesIntro.subtitle: Five verticals with smart contracts in production.

nft.name: Gaming & NFTs
nft.desc: True ownership, P2E economies, embedded royalties

industriesIntro.commonThreadBody: in each vertical a smart contract replaces a slow, intermediary-dependent process with code-enforced execution. We cover each, then NFT utility and DAOs, then six case studies, including one that was shut down.

defiWhat.heading: What is DeFi?
defiWhat.subtitle: Financial services run by smart contracts instead of institutions.
defiWhat.coreIdeaBody: Instead of a bank enforcing a loan or a clearinghouse settling a trade, a smart contract does it when conditions are met. This cuts fees and settlement time, and users keep custody of their assets.
defiWhat.valueCodeTitle: "Value and Code at the same level"
defiWhat.valueCodeBody: In traditional finance, the rules of trade live in legal documents and back-office systems separate from the money itself. In DeFi, value (ETH, USDC, NFTs) and the rules that govern it (the contract code) sit on the same blockchain — composable, atomic, transparent.

dex.name: DEXs / AMMs
dex.desc: Decentralized exchanges using liquidity pools (Uniswap, CoW Swap, Curve)

lending.name: Lending
lending.desc: Over-collateralized loans without credit checks (Aave, Compound)

stablecoins.name: Stablecoins
stablecoins.desc: Tokens pegged to USD/EUR (USDC, DAI, USDT) — global, programmable money

yield.name: Yield
yield.desc: Automated strategies that route deposits to highest-return pools (Yearn)

derivatives.name: Derivatives
derivatives.desc: Perpetuals, options, synthetics — trading without intermediaries (dYdX, GMX)

stablecoinsIntro.heading: Stablecoins
stablecoinsIntro.subtitle: Tokens designed to track a stable reference, almost always 1 USD. Three designs, three failure modes.

fiat.name: Fiat-backed
fiat.how: A company holds real dollars / T-bills in a bank and issues one token per dollar.
fiat.risk: You must trust the issuer and its reserves.

crypto.name: Crypto-collateralised
crypto.how: Users lock surplus crypto (e.g. $150 of ETH) in a contract to mint $100 of stablecoin.
crypto.risk: A sharp crash can under-collateralise and trigger liquidations.

algo.name: Algorithmic
algo.how: Code expands and contracts supply to chase the peg — no real assets behind it.
algo.risk: Reflexive: confidence loss spirals. UST/LUNA wiped out ~$40B in 2022.

stablecoinsIntro.nextBody: stress-test a peg yourself on the next slide.

pros.label: 24/7 Global Access
pros.desc: Markets, payments, and dollar-pegged balances stay open all day — no cut-off windows or borders.

pros.label: Instant Settlement
pros.desc: Trades and transfers clear in a single block (seconds), eliminating clearing delays.

pros.label: Reduced Costs
pros.desc: Smart contracts replace banks, card networks and brokers; fees on swaps and cross-border payments fall.

pros.label: Self-Custody
pros.desc: Users keep their own keys. Value moves peer-to-peer without frozen accounts or withdrawal limits.

pros.label: Predictable Value
pros.desc: Stablecoins let users hold and spend a token that maintains a fiat parity (mostly USD).

pros.label: Programmable Cash Flows
pros.desc: Code automates swaps, payouts, and recurring transfers once preset conditions are met.

pros.label: Permissionless Markets
pros.desc: Anyone can list and launch a new token pair or liquidity pool. No gatekeepers.

cons.label: Regulatory Uncertainty
cons.desc: Rules on KYC, securities status, and stablecoin backing differ by jurisdiction and keep evolving.

cons.label: Smart Contract Bugs
cons.desc: Technical vulnerabilities or exploits can drain pools, freeze funds, or break a stablecoin peg.

cons.label: Liquidity Fragmentation
cons.desc: Assets spread across many chains and pools. Big trades face slippage or thin depth.

cons.label: Peg Instability
cons.desc: Even "stable" coins can de-peg if reserves, collateral ratios, or algorithms fail.

cons.label: UX Complexity
cons.desc: Setting up wallets, safeguarding seed phrases, paying gas — all deter mainstream adoption.

cons.label: On/Off-Ramp Friction
cons.desc: Moving funds between banks and blockchain wallets still depends on centralized exchanges and KYC.

nftIntro.heading: What is an NFT?
nftIntro.subtitle: A unique digital asset recorded on-chain that certifies ownership and authenticity.
nftIntro.unlikeBodyB: — your 1 ETH equals my 1 ETH. NFTs are not. Each NFT has its own ID and metadata, recorded on the ERC-721 (or ERC-1155) standard. Owning the token means owning that specific asset.
nftIntro.gamingBody: NFTs can represent swords, skins, characters or virtual land. Because the NFT sits in the player's wallet, not on the publisher's server, it can be listed, traded or rented peer-to-peer.
gamingPoints: Royalty terms can be attached to the token

nftEconomies.heading: Ownership and virtual economies
nftEconomies.subtitle: Smart contracts turn server-side database rows into player-owned, transferable, programmable assets.

before.title: Before Web3
points: Digital assets lived on centralized servers, owned by publishers

No cross-game portability

withNft.title: With NFTs

Lend NFTs out for yield (like real-estate rental)

pros.label: True Digital Ownership
pros.desc: Items live in the player's wallet, can't be revoked, and survive server shutdowns.

pros.label: Player-Driven Economies
pros.desc: Open on-chain markets set prices; supply & demand determine value, not publishers.

pros.label: Programmable Cash Flows
pros.desc: Smart contracts automate rentals, revenue-sharing, staking, and collateralized lending.

pros.label: Global 24/7 Markets

pros.label: Composability
pros.desc: NFTs plug into DeFi or social dApps, unlocking governance, yield, or utility bonuses.

cons.label: Price Volatility

cons.label: Regulatory Gray Zones
cons.desc: Loot-box-style drops and token rewards may face gambling or securities scrutiny.

cons.label: UX Friction
cons.desc: Wallet setup, key management, and gas fees are barriers for mainstream gamers.

cons.label: Scams & Counterfeits
cons.desc: Phishing sites and fake collections trick players into signing malicious transactions.

cons.label: Game-Health Dependency
cons.desc: Asset value hinges on an active player base. If the game fades, prices collapse.

cons.label: Market Saturation

pros.label: Fractional Ownership
pros.desc: Small investors gain access to high-value real estate, art, or institutional funds with low capital.

pros.label: Increased Liquidity

pros.label: 24/7 Global Access
pros.desc: Investors participate from anywhere, any time — no broker hours, no geographic gating.

pros.label: Reduced Costs
pros.desc: Smart contracts automate compliance, transfer, and payout workflows — slashing administrative overhead.

pros.label: Transparent Records
pros.desc: Blockchain ensures tamper-proof title, transaction history, and audit trails.

pros.label: Programmable Cash Flows
pros.desc: Rental income, dividends, coupons distribute automatically via smart contracts.

pros.label: Faster Settlement
pros.desc: Property transfers and securities settlement compress from weeks to minutes/days.

cons.label: Regulatory Uncertainty

cons.label: Valuation Drift
cons.desc: On-chain token prices may diverge from underlying asset NAV — pricing reliability is an open problem.

pros.label: Transparency
pros.desc: All partners see the same tamper-proof ledger — eliminating information asymmetry.

pros.label: Real-Time Traceability
pros.desc: A product's full journey can be located within seconds — not days.

pros.label: Process Automation
pros.desc: Smart contracts trigger payments, releases, and alerts without manual checks.

pros.label: Faster Dispute Resolution
pros.desc: Shared data removes he-said-she-said — investigations and chargebacks shorten dramatically.

pros.label: Cost Reduction
pros.desc: Less paperwork, fewer courier fees, streamlined audits — overall overhead drops.

pros.label: Regulatory Compliance
pros.desc: Immutable logs provide instant evidence for food, pharma, and customs inspections.

pros.label: Consumer Trust
pros.desc: Shoppers scan a code to verify origin, quality, and handling conditions.

cons.label: Data-Input Integrity
cons.desc: "Garbage in, garbage forever" — bad sensor data still writes immutably to the chain.

cons.label: Integration Complexity
cons.desc: Legacy ERPs, IoT devices, and port systems require costly and complicated connections.

cons.label: Standard Fragmentation
cons.desc: Competing consortia hinder network effects and global interoperability.

cons.label: Implementation Cost
cons.desc: Sensors, middleware, and change management demand significant upfront investment.

cons.label: Scalability
cons.desc: Public chains may struggle with container-level transaction volumes.

cons.label: Stakeholder Coordination
cons.desc: Rival companies must cooperate. Adoption stalls if key partners refuse to participate.

pros.label: Tamper-Proof & Verifiable
pros.desc: Certificates are hashed and stored on-chain — making them immutable.

pros.label: Eliminates Forgery
pros.desc: Even single-character alterations are detectable. Reduces fake diplomas, licenses, and credentials to ~zero.

pros.label: No Intermediaries
pros.desc: Removes the need for notaries, registry offices, or institutional verification emails.

pros.label: Instant & Global
pros.desc: Recipients share credentials digitally; employers verify them in seconds, anywhere.

pros.label: Cost & Time Efficiency
pros.desc: No more printing, postage, manual checks. Issuance and verification accelerate dramatically.

pros.label: Self-Sovereignty
pros.desc: Users hold their own credentials — reducing institutional gatekeeping.

cons.label: Legal Recognition
cons.desc: In many countries, blockchain-based records aren't legally recognized as official proof.

cons.label: User Literacy
cons.desc: Users need basic knowledge of blockchain, wallets, or verification tools to participate.

cons.label: Implementation Cost
cons.desc: Setting up a robust certification system requires technical expertise and initial investment.

cons.label: Privacy Concerns
cons.desc: Even hashed metadata may leak personal information if not carefully designed.

cons.label: Revocation Complexity
cons.desc: Once written to a blockchain, it's permanent. Revoking or updating requires extra contract logic.

cons.label: Vendor Lock-in
cons.desc: Different consortia use different chains — interoperability still emerging.

quiz.question: The California DMV digitized 42 million vehicle titles on blockchain. What is the primary advantage of blockchain over the traditional paper title system?
options: Blockchain storage is cheaper than paper filing, reducing the DMV operating budget significantly.
Title transfers and ownership verification can occur in minutes without contacting the DMV — eliminating fraud via immutable provenance records.
Vehicle titles are now publicly visible to anyone without identity verification, increasing transparency.
Vehicle theft becomes impossible because titles are stored on-chain and cannot be cloned.
quiz.explanation: The core blockchain advantage here is trustless verification of ownership history. Traditional paper titles require physical transfer, manual verification, and weeks of processing. With blockchain, a buyer can instantly verify the full ownership chain, detect odometer fraud, and confirm the seller has clear title — all without trusting the DMV database or the seller's word. The immutability makes forgery structurally impossible rather than merely difficult. Blockchain storage is actually more expensive than paper — the value is in verification speed and fraud elimination, not cost.

takeaways.title: Section 03 — Key Takeaways
items: Five industry verticals — DeFi, Gaming/NFTs, RWA, Supply Chain, Digital Cert — all show smart contracts in production today
DeFi: AMMs, stablecoins and borderless transfers reshape financial rails — and each stablecoin design has its own failure mode
NFTs work best as keys, not pictures: tickets, memberships, credentials, provenance twins. Royalties were never enforced by the chain
DAOs can mimic a company transparently or build structures no charter allows — token votes, nested multisigs, quadratic funding, timelocks, rage-quit
DAO reality check: low turnout, whale power, legal exposure, governance attacks (Beanstalk) — and ConstitutionDAO's $47M lesson in planning for failure
RWA tokenization spans the spectrum from sovereign debt (BlackRock BUIDL) to real estate (Sweden, Brickblock, Zurich)
Supply chain wins when rivals agree to share truth — Walmart and GSBN run; Maersk's TradeLens shut down because competitors would not join
The common thread for success: many parties, no trusted authority, value from automation and shared truth — and an owner everyone can accept
Section 4 adds three lessons from the field: Estonia, The DAO and ASX

nftUtility.heading: NFTs Beyond Art: the Token as a Key
nftUtility.subtitle: An NFT is a transferable, verifiable record that this wallet holds this right. Rights are what businesses sell.

cards.title: Membership & clubs
cards.how: The NFT is the membership card. Resell it and the membership moves with it — the club earns on every resale.
cards.example: Flyfish Club: a New York restaurant whose membership is an NFT · VeeFriends conference access

cards.title: Gated content, shops & communities
cards.how: Prove you hold the token → unlock a Discord channel, a product drop, a file. Nothing to sign up for; the wallet is the login.
cards.example: Shopify tokengated commerce · Collab.Land Discord gating

cards.title: Tickets
cards.how: Each ticket is unique and verifiable at the door, with resale rules written into the contract — price caps, identity binding, a cut to the artist.
cards.example: GET Protocol (millions of NFT tickets issued) · Ticketmaster token-gated sales (2023)

cards.title: Credentials & attendance
cards.how: Proof you were there or earned it — a badge nobody can forge or quietly revoke. Non-transferable ("soulbound") versions suit diplomas and KYC.
cards.example: POAP (millions of attendance badges since 2019) · soulbound tokens

cards.title: Digital twins for physical goods
cards.how: A watch, sneaker or handbag gets a token that travels with it through resale — warranty, service history and authenticity in one record.
cards.example: Breitling digital passports (Arianee) · LVMH Aura (see Supply Chain)

cards.title: Loyalty & brand engagement
cards.how: Points become collectibles fans can trade; brands reach customers' wallets directly. Big names tried it — and most pilots have since closed.
cards.example: Starbucks Odyssey (Dec 2022 → closed Mar 2024) · Nike .SWOOSH / RTFKT (wound down 2024)

nftUtility.patternBody: the NFT is rarely the product. It is the key that unlocks one, and keys are portable, verifiable and resellable.

nftGate.title: Token-gated access · Try it
nftGate.subtitle: Pick a wallet and try to enter the members-only area. The gate never asks who you are — only what you hold.

wrong.name: Wallet B
wrong.holds: Holds an NFT — from a different collection

steps.label: Prove control
steps.desc: The wallet signs a one-time message. No password, no account — the signature proves you hold the key.

steps.label: Read the chain
steps.desc: The gate asks the membership contract: how many tokens does this address hold? A free read — no transaction, no gas.

steps.label: Decide
steps.desc: Balance ≥ 1 → the door opens. Otherwise → denied. The content itself stays on an ordinary server.

nftGate.deniedWrong: Denied: that token is from another collection
nftGate.deniedEmpty: Denied: no membership token in this wallet
nftGate.idle: Choose a wallet and click enter
nftGate.noteBody: no customer database to breach, membership that customers can resell, and one key that works across every partner who reads the same contract.

nftHonest.heading: The Honest NFT Story
nftHonest.subtitle: The 2021 boom promised perpetual royalties and a new creator economy. What happened, and what survived.

cards.title: Royalties were never enforced by the chain
cards.body: ERC-2981 only declares a royalty; the marketplace decides whether to pay it. When Blur competed on zero royalties (2022), OpenSea made them optional (2023). Creator royalty income fell by more than 90% from its early-2022 peak.
cards.lesson: A business model that depends on marketplaces volunteering to pay is not enforced by code.

cards.title: Volume was inflated by wash trading
cards.body: Selling a token to yourself from a second wallet pumps "floor prices" and farms marketplace token rewards. Analysts estimate tens of billions of dollars of 2022 reported NFT volume was wash trades.
cards.lesson: On-chain data is transparent — but transparent is not the same as true. Read volume like any unaudited number.

cards.title: Most of the asset isn't on-chain
cards.body: The token is on-chain; the image or file usually sits on a server or IPFS, referenced by a link. If the host disappears, the token points at nothing.
cards.lesson: Ask what the token actually controls: a right, an access, a record — or a URL.

cards.title: What survived
cards.body: Ticketing, provenance twins, credentials and token-gating: uses where the token is a key, not a speculation.
cards.lesson: Utility that does not depend on the price going up is the utility that lasts.

daoIntro.heading: What is a DAO?
daoIntro.subtitle: An organisation whose rulebook is a smart contract: members propose and vote, and the treasury acts on the result — no CEO signs off.
daoIntro.tradEnforced: Enforced by bylaws, courts and HR — mostly behind closed doors.
daoIntro.daoEnforced: Enforced by code — every vote, payment and rule change is public forever.
daoIntro.twoLabel: Two things a DAO can do
daoIntro.mimicBody: Shareholder votes, committees, spending limits, dual signatures: the familiar structures, with no backdated minutes, no quiet transfers, and an audit trail nobody can edit.
daoIntro.newBody: Votes that cost more the more you cast, committees that are themselves contracts, mandatory delays that let members exit before a rule bites, instant withdrawal of your share. New organisational designs — with new failure modes.
daoIntro.defBody: "Autonomous" is generous: people still write proposals, debate on forums and vote. What is automatic is the execution — the money moves because the vote passed, not because someone approved it.

daoStructures.title: Governance building blocks · Explore
daoStructures.subtitle: Click a block. Some copy structures every company has; others are only possible in code. Real DAOs combine four or five of them.

tokenVote.name: Token-weighted voting
tokenVote.analogy: One share, one vote at the AGM
tokenVote.how: Each governance token is one vote. A proposal passes when it clears a quorum and a majority — counted by the contract, not a registrar.
tokenVote.example: Uniswap: UNI holders vote; 40M UNI quorum
tokenVote.risk: Whales dominate, and turnout is often under 10% of tokens.

multisig.name: Multisig wallet
multisig.analogy: A bank account needing 3 of 5 directors' signatures
multisig.how: Funds move only when M of N named keys approve. Used for treasuries, emergency powers and admin keys.
multisig.example: Most DAO treasuries sit in a Safe multisig
multisig.risk: Signers are identifiable people — pressure, lost keys, collusion.

nested.name: Nested multisigs & sub-DAOs
nested.analogy: A holding company with subsidiaries — but every layer is code
nested.how: A signer on the main multisig can itself be a multisig or a sub-DAO with its own vote. Budgets flow down; accountability flows up — all on-chain.
nested.example: MakerDAO Core Units & SubDAOs · Arbitrum Security Council (9 of 12)
nested.risk: Complexity hides power; few members can map who controls what.

quadratic.name: Quadratic voting & funding
quadratic.how: Casting n votes costs n² tokens, so 10,000 tokens buy only 100 votes. Dampens plutocracy — if every voter is one real person.
quadratic.example: Gitcoin Grants matches small donations quadratically
quadratic.risk: Sybil attacks: split one wallet into 100 to look like 100 people. Needs identity (Gitcoin Passport).

timelock.name: Timelock
timelock.analogy: A 30-day notice period before a rule change
timelock.how: An approved proposal executes only after a fixed delay, often 24–72 hours. Dissenters can exit; attackers cannot drain a treasury instantly.
timelock.example: Compound & Uniswap: 2-day Timelock · MakerDAO's GSM pause
timelock.risk: Slows emergency response — which is why many DAOs add a guardian multisig.

roles.name: Roles, councils & guardians
roles.analogy: A board that can act between AGMs; a CEO's emergency veto
roles.how: Elected councils hold scoped powers — pause, grants, upgrades — under rules set by the token vote. The contracts' access control enforces who may do what.
roles.example: Optimism Token House + Citizens' House · Aave Guardian
roles.risk: Recreates the hierarchy the DAO promised to remove — the question is whether it is transparent.

ragequit.name: Rage-quit (exit rights)
ragequit.analogy: Closest: redeeming a fund share — at the speed of code
ragequit.how: A member who loses a vote can burn their shares and withdraw their proportional slice of the treasury before the decision executes.
ragequit.example: Moloch DAO (2019) and its many forks
ragequit.risk: The treasury can shrink suddenly; works best for small, aligned groups.

daoVote.title: Who really holds the power?
daoVote.subtitle: Five members vote on the same proposal. Change the counting rule — and watch who wins.
daoVote.proposal: Proposal: spend 10% of the treasury on a marketing campaign

token.name: 1 token = 1 vote
token.lesson: Capital decides. Defensible when the vote is about money at risk — but one whale outvotes four members.

quadratic.name: Quadratic (√ tokens)
quadratic.lesson: Dampens the whale — but only if every wallet is a distinct person. Split the whale into 100 wallets and it wins again (the Sybil problem).

person.name: 1 person = 1 vote
person.lesson: Egalitarian — but needs proof of personhood, and a member holding 50 tokens outweighs one holding 5,000.

daoVote.clickHint: Click a member to flip their vote

daoExamples.heading: Real DAOs: what works, what broke
daoExamples.subtitle: Five organisations, five structures, five lessons. Note how much governance happens on forums and in multisigs — not just in the vote.

items.name: MakerDAO → Sky
items.what: Issues the DAI stablecoin (and now USDS); token holders set collateral rules and interest rates.
items.structure: Token vote → executive "spell" → GSM timelock. Core Units and SubDAOs run operations; an Emergency Shutdown exists as a last resort.
items.lesson: The longest-running DeFi DAO shows governance can work — and that it drifts toward professional delegates and complex structures.

items.name: Uniswap DAO
items.what: Governs the Uniswap protocol and a multi-billion-dollar UNI treasury.
items.structure: Snapshot temperature check → on-chain vote (40M UNI quorum) → 2-day Timelock. Most UNI is delegated to a few dozen delegates.
items.lesson: Years of debate over switching on a protocol "fee switch" show how slow and political token governance can be.

items.name: Gitcoin
items.what: Funds open-source and public-goods projects through community rounds — tens of millions of dollars distributed.
items.structure: Quadratic funding: many small donations attract more matching than one big cheque. Gitcoin Passport fights fake identities.
items.lesson: A funding rule that is impossible to run without code — and a live, ongoing fight against Sybil attacks.

items.name: ConstitutionDAO
items.what: In Nov 2021, 17,000+ people pooled ~$47M in ETH in under a week to bid on a rare copy of the US Constitution at Sotheby's.
items.structure: A multisig held the funds; contributors got PEOPLE tokens. No plan for custody of the document — or for losing.
items.lesson: Outbid by a single billionaire. Refunds cost small donors more in gas than they had given. Coordination worked; governance and operations did not.

items.name: The DAO (2016)
items.what: A crowd-funded venture fund run entirely by contract — the largest crowdfund of its time.
items.structure: Token vote on investments; a "split" function with a reentrancy bug and no pause button.
items.lesson: Drained of $60M; Ethereum hard-forked to undo it. Full story in Section 4 — Three Lessons.

daoExamples.legalBody: Wyoming recognises DAO LLCs (2021), but a US court treated Ooki DAO's token voters as members of an unincorporated association — personally exposed to its liabilities (2022–23). Most serious DAOs now pair the contracts with a legal wrapper.

pros.label: Transparency by default
pros.desc: Every vote, payment and rule change is public and permanent — no backdated minutes.

pros.label: Global membership
pros.desc: Anyone with a wallet can join, contribute and vote — no incorporation, no bank account.

pros.label: Programmable treasury
pros.desc: Budgets, vesting and payouts execute from the vote — no finance department in the loop.

pros.label: Hard to cheat
pros.desc: Spending limits and signature rules are enforced by code, not by whoever holds the chequebook.

pros.label: Minority protection
pros.desc: Timelocks and rage-quit let dissenters exit before a decision bites — rare in company law.

pros.label: New coordination tools
pros.desc: Quadratic funding, nested sub-DAOs, instant pooled capital — structures a charter cannot express.

cons.label: Voter apathy
cons.desc: Turnout is often under 10% of tokens; a few dozen delegates decide most votes.

cons.label: Plutocracy
cons.desc: Token-weighted means money-weighted. Whales and VCs can carry any vote they care about.

cons.label: Legal exposure
cons.desc: Unincorporated DAOs may leave members personally liable (Ooki DAO). Wrappers add back lawyers and jurisdictions.

cons.label: Slow in a crisis
cons.desc: Timelocks protect members but tie hands. The DAO had 27 days' warning and still could not act.

cons.label: Governance attacks
cons.desc: Beanstalk (2022): an attacker flash-loaned 67% of the votes, passed a proposal and drained $182M in one transaction.

cons.label: Off-chain reality
cons.desc: Forums, Discord, lawyers and core teams do the real work. The chain records the decision; people make it.

tradelens.heading: TradeLens: Maersk × IBM
tradelens.subtitle: A global shipping-data platform with blue-chip backers — discontinued in 2023 after five years. The technology worked; the business model didn't.
tradelens.problemBodyB: and a paper trail that has barely changed in decades:
problemPoints: Bills of lading, certificates and customs forms couriered or e-mailed between carriers, ports, forwarders and banks
No shared view of where the cargo or its documents are
Discrepancies take days of phone calls to reconcile
Fraud and lost documents are routine
tradelens.problemCostBody: Documentation estimated at up to a fifth of the cost of moving goods
tradelens.solutionBodyB: on Hyperledger Fabric — a permissioned ledger shared by the whole trade ecosystem:
solutionPoints: Shipping events and documents published once, visible to every authorised party
Electronic bills of lading and customs filings on the same platform
100+ organisations joined, including several of the world's largest carriers
Technically sound, well funded, live in production
tradelens.solutionFlow: Event logged once → shared with all parties → documents follow the cargo
happenedPoints: Nov 2022: Maersk and IBM announce discontinuation; the platform is wound down by early 2023
Official reason: it "did not reach the level of commercial viability necessary"
Rival carriers were reluctant to feed data into a platform owned by their biggest competitor
Value required near-universal participation — a network-effect and ownership problem, not a technology problem
tradelens.lessonBody: a consortium chain is only as useful as the rivals willing to join it. Who owns the platform decides who adopts it — compare GSBN, owned jointly by several carriers, which is still running.

keyPoints.s3-industries-intro: Every working use case here replaces a slow, paid-for middleman with a shared rule.
keyPoints.s3-defi-intro: DeFi replaces the bank or clearinghouse with a contract that settles when its conditions are met.
keyPoints.s3-defi-amm: Price comes from a formula, so big trades move it; liquidity depth is the product.
keyPoints.s3-defi-stablecoins: Every stablecoin design is a bet on what backs the dollar.
keyPoints.s3-defi-prosCons: DeFi removes the bank but moves the risk into code, collateral and admin keys.
keyPoints.s3-nft-intro: An NFT is a unique token whose owner is recorded on-chain, so ownership can be proved and transferred without the issuer.
keyPoints.s3-nft-real: The NFT only records ownership; the servers, artwork and marketplace are still run by companies.
keyPoints.s3-nft-prosCons: Ownership you can prove and resell is new; demand for the asset is not guaranteed by the blockchain.
keyPoints.s3-nft-utility: An NFT is a key, not a picture; tickets, memberships and credentials are where the utility is.
keyPoints.s3-nft-gate: A membership card that the club can't secretly revoke and you can resell.
keyPoints.s3-nft-honest: Royalties and floor prices were promises by marketplaces and founders; only what the contract enforces survived.
keyPoints.s3-dao-intro: Code enforces the rules, but people still choose them; governance design is the product.
keyPoints.s3-dao-structures: Each building block trades speed for legitimacy: a multisig is fast, a token vote is fair, a timelock protects both.
keyPoints.s3-dao-vote: Ask who holds power after launch — not who promised what before it.
keyPoints.s3-dao-examples: Even successful DAOs are run by a small active group; low turnout and whale votes are the norm.
keyPoints.s3-dao-prosCons: A DAO buys transparency and global participation at the cost of speed, legal clarity and attack surface.
keyPoints.s3-rwa-spectrum: The simpler the legal claim, the easier the token; treasuries went first, real estate comes last.
keyPoints.s3-rwa-real: BlackRock and a national land registry are on-chain because settlement time and reconciliation cost are measurable.
keyPoints.s3-rwa-prosCons: A token moves in seconds, but the legal title it represents moves at the speed of the law.
keyPoints.s3-sc-provenance: The chain proves who recorded what and when; it cannot prove the goods match the record.
keyPoints.s3-sc-real: These work because rivals agreed to share one record; the hard part was the consortium, not the code.
keyPoints.s3-sc-prosCons: Traceability pays when recalls, counterfeits or paperwork are expensive, and only if every partner uploads.
keyPoints.s3-cert-howitworks: Store the fingerprint, not the document: a hash proves a record existed unchanged without revealing it.
keyPoints.s3-cert-real: The chain lets anyone verify a record without calling the issuer.
keyPoints.s3-cert-prosCons: Verification becomes instant and free; the issuer's honesty when creating the record is still the weak point.
keyPoints.s3-case-gallery: Five production deployments share one pattern: many parties, one shared record, and a measurable cost that disappeared.
keyPoints.s3-tradelens: Rivals would not join a platform owned by their biggest competitor.
keyPoints.s3-exercise: Pain point, parties, trigger, output, risk: fill all five in a sentence each.
